text:
Bouchard c. Succession de
Zalac

2023 QCCS 3495

SUPERIOR COURT

(Civil
Division)

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT of

montréal

N° :

500-17-117315-211

DATE :

SEPTEMBER 6, 2023

______________________________________________________________________

in the presence of the

honorable

guylène
beaugé, j.s.c.

______________________________________________________________________

LINDA MARIE BRUNA BOUCHARD

Plaintiff

vs.

THE ESTATE OF SLAVOLJUB ZALAC

Defendant

and

BORIS ZALAC

Mis en cause

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

1.

PREVIEW

[
1
]

The Plaintiff Linda Marie Bruna Bouchard and the
late Slavoljub Zalac who were in a common-law relationship since 1986 got
married in 2001. No children were born issue of their relationship.

[
2
]

The late Zalac had previously been married to
Ms. Ljubica Zilbak, with whom he had two children, Richard, and the mis en
cause Boris Zalac. Following his divorce, the late Zalac entered in a common-law
relationship with Ms. Danuta Jesiolowska, with whom he had another child,
Steve Junior Jesiolowska.

[
3
]

On November 10, 2015, the late Zalac executed a
Last Will and Testament before a notary (the “
2015 WILL
”) in which he designated the Plaintiff as
liquidator of his estate and made her his sole universal legatee. Should she
precede him, he designated his son Richard Zalac to replace her as the liquidator
and bequeathed to his three sons in equal shares all his property movable and
immovable.

[
4
]

On September 24, 2020, the late Zalac executed a
new Last Will and Testament before a notary (the “
2020 WILL
”) according to which he bequeathed the universality
of his property to his son Boris Zalac and appointed him liquidator of his
estate. Should the later predecease him, the late Zalac designated his common-law
spouse Gilles Bourgeois as liquidator of his estate and made his son Richard
Zalac his universal legatee.

[
5
]

The late Zalac passed away on March 5, 2021, at 87
years old.

[
6
]

Claiming that the 2020 Will was signed under
undue influence from Boris Zalac, the Plaintiff asks that it be declared null
and void. In her Modified Application, she also asks that Boris Zalac be
declared unworthy of benefiting from the late Zalac’s estate (the “
ESTATE
”).

[
7
]

The freedom to test is absolute. However, even
if a will is a unilateral act, the testator’s consent may be vitiated by undue
influence. In the absence of a definition in the
Civil Code of Quebec
,
consistent case law since a leading judgment of the Supreme Court
[1]
holds that undue influence (or “
captation
” in French) consists of fraudulent
maneuvers intended to induce a person to bequeath in a certain way. That case
law specifies that it is not illegal to curry favour with a testator through
zeal or displays of affection, even for selfish purposes. It is, however,
illicit to take advantage of this proximity to seize the will of a person, and
to suggest how to bequeath.

[
8
]

Undue influence is sometimes exercised in an
obvious way. It can also result from a series of behaviours which are not
determining, but which, combined, constitute influence of a fraudulent nature. The
behaviour that the case law associates with undue influence varies from case to
case. However, courts generally will consider the testator’s age and state of
health to assess his vulnerability or his ability to resist to fraudulent
tactics.

[
9
]

Where there is no direct evidence of undue
influence, it can be inferred from proof established by presumption of facts,
because the ill-intentioned legatee will unlikely act openly. The Court will
then verify whether this proof establishes, on a balance of probabilities,
serious, precise, and concordant presumptions
[2]
making
the thesis of undue influence probable. If so, and if the legatee’s maneuvers induced
the decision of the testator, the will shall be set aside.

[
10
]

For the reasons set out below, the Court finds
that the Plaintiff has met her burden to establish, on a balance of
probabilities, that Boris Zalac exercised undue influence onto the deceased.
The 2020 Will shall therefore be declared null and void, and the devolution of
the Estate executed according to the 2015 Will.

[
11
]

However, the Court will not grant the conclusion
seeking the declaration of unworthiness. That conclusion is moot since the 2015
Will does not make Boris Zalac a legatee. Moreover, the Plaintiff added that
conclusion in her Modified Application dated July 22, 2022. Consequently, it
must fail because the Plaintiff did not apply within one year after the opening
of the succession or becoming aware of a cause of unworthiness (
Article 623

of the
Civil Code of Quebec
).

2.

CONTEXT

[
12
]

Linda Bouchard was born in 1954 and the late
Zalac in 1933. They met in the early eighties through the latter’s son Boris
Zalac who was a friend of Ms. Bouchard. At the time, she was 22 years old,
and the late Zalac was in his mid forties.

[
13
]

The late Zalac was divorced from his first wife
with whom he had two sons, Richard, and Boris. He was in a common-law
relationship with the mother of his third and youngest son, Steve Jr.

[
14
]

Around 1985, the late Zalac separated and
started dating Ms. Bouchard. She moved in with him in his home on [Avenue
A], in Montreal. In 1986, the late Zalac sold that house and bought another
property in Roxboro in which he lived with Ms. Bouchard until 1989.

[
15
]

In 1989, Ms. Bouchard and the late Zalac
moved as tenants in a property located on [...], in Notre-Dame-de-Grâce. That
property, part of a quadruplex which was built by Ms. Bouchard’s grandfather
in the thirties, was owned by her mother.

[
16
]

On June 21, 1995, the late Zalac executed the
1995 Will before a lawyer, Mtre David Rosenzveig. It provides that Ms. Bouchard
is the liquidator of the Estate, Mtre Rosenzveig to replace her if she
predeceased him or is unable to act as such. Moreover, Ms. Bouchard is
constituted the sole universal heir.

[
17
]

On November 24, 2001, Ms. Bouchard and the
late Zalac got married. His sons were not informed nor invited to the wedding.

[
18
]

On October 9, 2002, Ms. Bouchard and the
late Zalac purchased each one undivided half of the apartment they were renting
on [Street A] with the help of Ms. Bouchard’s mother who gifted her a
discount on the value of the property.

[
19
]

On November 28, 2003, Ms. Bouchard and the
late Zalac purchased one undivided half of a rental immovable located at [...].
Ms. Bouchard’s mother gifted her $40,000 toward the purchase price and the
balance was paid with a loan.

[
20
]

In 2004, the late Zalac retired, and Ms. Bouchard
continued to work.

[
21
]

On November 30, 2013, the late Zalac gave
Plaintiff power of attorney over all his bank accounts.

[
22
]

On November 10, 2015, the late Zalac and Ms. Bouchard
each executed a Last Will and Testament before notary Line Martin (the “
2015
WILLS
”). Those wills
constitute mirror wills as to their main provisions: each is appointed
liquidator of the other’s estate and is named as universal legatee.

[
23
]

On January 17, 2019, Ms. Bouchard and the
late Zalac bought each one undivided half of the upper floor property located
at 996 Addington from Ms. Bouchard’s father’s estate. They took a mortgage
on the property.

[
24
]

On September 24, 2020, the late Zalac executed the
2020 Will before the notary Erika Teasdale: he removed Ms. Bouchard, appointed
Boris Zalac liquidator, and named him his sole universal legatee. Should Boris
Zalac predecease him, his spouse Gilles Bourgeois is to replace him, and Richard
Zalac becomes the universal legatee.

[
25
]

The late Zalac was scheduled to have a hip
replacement on March 2, 2021. He passed away on March 5 to colon cancer.

3.

ISSUES

[
26
]

The issues raised for determination are the
following:

-

Was the late Slavoljub Zalac the object of undue
influence (
captation
) on the part of the mis en cause Boris Zalac?

-

Is the mis en cause Boris Zalac unworthy of
inheriting?

4.

ANALYSIS

4.1

Undue influence

[
27
]

Ms. Bouchard contends that the 2020 Will
must be set aside and declared null and void on the grounds of undue influence
on the part of the mis en cause Boris Zalac.

4.1.1

The principles applicable

[
28
]

In
Brusenbauch
v.
Young
[3]
,
the Court of Appeal expounds the legal
framework applicable to the concept of undue influence:

[33] Likewise, he did not err in
expounding the legal framework applicable to the concept of
“
undue influence” as defined earlier (supra, para.
[16]). Professors Beaulne and Morin, commenting on the case law, explain as
follows:

690. – Captation ou suggestion. – Le dol ne figure plus dans la
liste des vices de consentement. Il n’en est question qu’à l’
article 1401

C.c.Q.
, qui semble indiquer que le dol n’est plus un vice de consentement autonome:
on ne le prendrait en considération, dans les contrats, que lorsque, émanant
d’une partie ou à sa connaissance, il provoque l’erreur de l’autre partie.
Comme le testament est un acte unilatéral, l’article 1401 C.c.Q. ne lui est pas
applicable. On doit néanmoins considérer qu’un testament peut être annulé pour
dol, c’est-à-dire lorsqu’il y a eu des manœuvres frauduleuses et que celles-ci
ont réellement provoqué la décision du testateur. Dans les libéralités, dans
les testaments en particulier, on parle souvent en l’occurrence de captation et
de suggestion, expressions empruntées à l’Ancien Droit.

691
. –
Nécessité de manœuvres
frauduleuses. – Il n’est pas illicite en soi de s’attirer la faveur du
testateur. Ainsi, le fait de déployer beaucoup de zèle envers un malade ou de
multiplier les témoignages d’affection à son égard, alors qu’en fait on cherche
à se faire instituer légataire, n’est pas en soi une cause de nullité, non plus
le fait d’appeler un notaire et de lui donner des directives quant au testament
à préparer. Comme l’exprimait la Cour d’appel :

Pour établir la captation, il faut prouver l’existence de manœuvres
dolosives ou frauduleuses. Il ne suffit pas de faire la démonstration que la
personne a simplement essayé de s’attirer les faveurs de la testatrice ou dans
le cas de Ronald, exprimé son désir de devenir propriétaire de la résidence
dans laquelle il habitait avec sa mère.

692. – Les faits de captation deviennent cependant dolosifs
lorsqu’ils s’accompagnent de pratiques artificieuses, comme l’interception de
correspondance ou le fait d’écarter les visites, ou encore le dénigrement
systématique à l’adresse des proches parents. C’est ce qu’a rappelé la Cour
dans l’affaire Gauthier :

Les défendeurs ont dépassé les simples suggestions ou conseils au
testateur. Leur attitude présente un caractère dolosif entraînant la nullité du
testament, puisque ces défendeurs se sont emparés de la volonté du testateur
pour lui suggérer comment tester […]

693. – Encore faut-il que les manœuvres frauduleuses aient été
déterminantes du consentement. Il faut donc établir un lien de causalité entre
les gestes posés par la personne accusée de captation et le contenu du
testament, car il est essentiel que ces gestes aient eu une influence sur le
consentement du testateur. C’est toujours à celui qui allègue la captation de
la prouver, et de simples soupçons ne suffisent pas à l’établir: il « […] doit
convaincre le Tribunal qu’elle a été déterminante sur les volontés exprimées
dans le testament attaqué ». La preuve peut être indirecte, mais elle doit être
prépondérante.
[...].

(References omitted)

[
29
]

As for the issue of the burden of proof, the
Court of Appeal comments as follows in
Brusenbauch
:

[15]

Since there is no controversy in the case law or among
authors on this topic nor is there disagreement between the parties to this
appeal, I will deal first, briefly, with the evidentiary standard in matters of
undue influence, such matters being highly factual.

[
16]

The rule is that which applies in all civil matters, unless the law provides
otherwise: the party who alleges undue influence (“
captation
”), which
implies fraud (“
dol
”) and c
onsequently, a defect in consent,
must establish both, as well as causation, on a
balance of probabilities, according to articles 2803 and 2804
C.C.Q.
[…]

[17]

The party alleging undue influence will discharge that
burden by direct or, more often (undue influence generally being a secret or
covert affair), circumstantial evidence, meaning evidence of facts – improper
schemes, disgraceful devices, lies, slander, deceit and trickery, or deliberate
misrepresentations – that constitute precise and concordant presumptions (art. 2849
C.C.Q.
)
and support such a finding.

(References omitted)

[
30
]

In
M.P.
c.
F.D
.
[4]
, Madam Justice Johanne Brodeur, j.s.c. provides a complete
explanation of the applicable principles in a case of alleged undue influence:

[27]   L’
article 704
du
Code
civil du Québec
décrit le testament comme étant un acte juridique
unilatéral révocable. Le testament exprime les volontés individuelles du
testateur qui souhaite régler la dévolution de ses biens à son décès, autrement
que ne le feraient les règles de dévolution légale.

[28]   Comme en matière de
contrats, le consentement du testateur doit être libre et éclairé. Il peut être
vicié par l’erreur ou la crainte. L’
article 1401

C.c.Q.
prévoit que
l’erreur provoquée par le dol vicie le consentement. Dans la mesure où le
consentement d’un testateur est vicié, ce ne sont plus réellement ses volontés
qui se retrouvent dans le testament.

[29]   Le comportement dolosif peut
provenir du bénéficiaire, mais également d’une personne qui n’a pas d’intérêt
au testament. Il n’est pas nécessaire de démontrer que le bénéficiaire est le
véritable auteur de la captation, l’important est de prouver que le
consentement a été extorqué.

[30]   Lorsque le testament ne
représente pas l’expression libre de la volonté du testateur et qu’il y a
démonstration d’un comportement mensonger, utilisation de ruses ou
comportements cherchant à enlever l’affection envers l’héritier présumé pour
lui ravir plus sûrement sa part d’héritage, il est alors nécessaire de conclure
à la présence de captation ce qui mène à la nullité du testament.

[31]   Comme l’écrivait l’auteur
Châteauguay Perrault « les mots « suggestion et captation » illustrent assez
bien de quoi il s’agit : quelqu’un s’empare de la volonté du testateur et lui
suggère comment il doit tester ».

[32]   La Cour d’appel a récemment
rappelé que les règles du
Code civil
en matière successorale doivent
être lues, comme la disposition préliminaire du
Code
l’indique, en
harmonie avec la
Charte des droits et libertés de la personne
. Les

articles 48
et
49
de la
Charte
se lisent comme suit :

48. Toute
personne âgée ou toute personne handicapée a droit d’être protégée contre toute
forme d’exploitation.

Telle personne a
aussi droit à la protection et à la sécurité que doivent lui apporter sa
famille ou les personnes qui en tiennent lieu.

49. Une atteinte
illicite à un droit ou à une liberté reconnu par la présente
Charte
confère à
la victime le droit d’obtenir la cessation de cette atteinte et la réparation
du préjudice moral ou matériel qui en résulte.

En cas d’atteinte illicite et
intentionnelle, le tribunal peut en outre condamner son auteur à des
dommages-intérêts punitifs.

[33]   Ainsi les personnes âgées
conservent certes, la faculté de tester, mais la protection déjà offerte contre
les manœuvres dolosives prévues au
Code
se trouve renforcée.

[34]   À ce sujet, ainsi s’exprime
le juge Rochon dans un arrêt de la Cour d’appel de 2012 :

[
47] La personne âgée et malade a certes le droit d’être
protégée contre toute forme d’exploitation, mais elle conserve également le
droit d’être généreuse envers ceux qui l’accompagnent dans cette période de fin
de vie. L’
article 48
de la
Charte
a été conçu dans une perspective de
protection de la personne âgée, mais non dans celle d’une perte de droits. À
cet égard, les propos du professeur Grimaldi me semblent justes :

« Il ne faut pas retirer
la liberté de disposer à titre gratuit, et singulièrement la liberté
testamentaire, à ceux auxquels elle est la plus secourable : aux personnes
âgées. Il ne faut pas les priver de ce qui les occupe et qui leur permet de
croire qu’elles se survivront à elles-mêmes : il serait inhumain d’imposer, à
partir d’un certain âge, comme un permis de donner ou de tester. »

[48] Je ne crois pas que l’application de l’article
48 entraîne nécessairement la perte du droit de donner. Il faut plutôt parler
de limite à ce droit, et ce, en fonction des circonstances de chaque affaire. »

[35]   Malheureusement, cet arrêt
ne fut pas soumis et les dispositions de la
Charte
ne furent pas
invoquées.

[36]   En 2018, la Cour d’appel a
réitéré que :

« Celui ou celle qui invoque la captation
doit en faire la preuve en démontrant qu’on s’est emparé de la volonté du testateur
et que les gestes posés l’ont, de façon déterminante, amené à signer un
testament qui n’aurait pas signé autrement. Ses gestes doivent s’apparenter à
de la fraude. Des manifestations de dévouement -sincère ou simulé - de nature à
susciter l’affection ne sont pas suffisantes. »

[37]   L’auteur Châteauguay
Perrault, dans un texte souvent cité en jurisprudence, identifie certains
éléments d’analyse :

« Mais ce qui doit être considéré comme
suggestion et captation pourra varier d’un cas à l’autre, selon les
circonstances particulières propres à l’affaire soumise. L’âge, l’état de
santé, la condition sociale, du testateur pourront avoir joué un rôle quant au
degré de résistance qu’il pouvait opposer aux manœuvres dont il était l’objet
».

[38]   Une revue des jugements
ayant conclu à la captation, nous permet de constater que l’un ou généralement
plus d’un fait suivant ont été retenus comme indice de captation :

−   l’avocat ou le notaire est choisi par l’héritier;

−  l’héritier joue un rôle actif dans la confection du
testament notamment lorsqu’il donne lui-même les directives;

−  la personne désignée au testament est présente avec le
notaire au moment du testament;

−  les héritiers potentiels ne sont pas avisés des
hospitalisations ou de la vraie nature de la maladie du testateur;

−  les liens entre l’héritier désigné et le testateur
s’intensifient et deviennent quasi exclusifs;

−  l’héritier obtient une procuration générale qu’il utilise
que la situation le requière ou non. Ce dernier confond les biens du testateur
avec les siens et se place en conflit d’intérêts durant la gestion;

−  l’héritier ne rend pas compte de l’administration faite par
lui des biens du donateur de son vivant ou en tant que liquidateur après décès;

−  le liquidateur s’empresse de partager les biens après le
décès;

−  le testateur est vulnérable au moment ou durant la période
qui précède le testament;

−  l’héritier s’immisce dans les affaires du testateur;

−  il existe entre l’héritier et les autres membres de la
famille ou héritiers potentiels des tensions ou du ressentiment;

−  l’héritier avise tardivement les membres de la famille, du
décès;

− l’héritier isole le testateur et fait preuve d’une intention
et de prévenance intéressée ainsi que d’altruisme;

−  l’héritier tente d’effacer de la mémoire du testateur les
autres héritiers potentiels; par le retrait des cadeaux donnés par eux, le
retrait de photos les représentant ou l’interception de correspondance;

−  l’héritier est nommé liquidateur;

−  avant le décès, l’héritier reçoit des dons ou avantages;

− un changement subit d’attitude du testateur s’opère face aux
tiers et autres héritiers potentiels;

−  il y a omniprésence et influence de l’héritier auprès du
testateur;

−  le testament reflète ce que l’héritier croit juste et
légitime;

− l’héritier calomnie les héritiers présomptifs et irrite le
testateur contre ces personnes;

−  l’héritier fait état ou exagère sa situation économique
difficile;

−  plus d’un testament ou codicilles sont préparés;

−  les membres de la famille et autres tiers ne sont pas
avisés des funérailles qui sont tenues dans la plus stricte intimité afin
d’éviter aux héritiers de répondre aux questions concernant le testament et
pour conserver le maximum de capital dans la succession.

(References omitted)

[
31
]

Moreover, at paragraph 39 and following, she
sets out the analysis grid for presumptions of fact developed by the Court of
Appeal in
Barrette
[5]
:

[39]   Celui qui invoque le vice de
consentement d’un testament doit en faire la preuve, selon la balance des probabilités.

[40]   La captation peut être
prouvée par tous moyens de preuve notamment par présomptions. Ce dernier moyen
de preuve est généralement celui retenu, car les manœuvres frauduleuses sont
toujours conduites dans le secret.

[41]   L’
article 2849
du
C.c.Q.

prévoit que les présomptions de fait sont laissées à l’appréciation du tribunal
qui ne doit prendre en considération que celles qui sont graves, précises et
concordantes. L’hypothèse, la conjoncture, la spéculation et les soupçons ne
sont pas suffisants pour faire naître une présomption de fait.

Les
présomptions sont graves, lorsque les rapports du fait connu au fait inconnu
sont tels que l’existence de l’un établit, par une induction puissante,
l’existence de l’autre…

Les
présomptions sont précises, lorsque les inductions qui résultent du fait connu
tendent à établir directement et particulièrement le fait inconnu et contesté…

Elles
sont enfin concordantes, lorsque, ayant toutes une origine commune ou
différente, elles tendent, par leur ensemble et leur accord, à établir le fait
qu’il s’agit de prouver… Si au contraire, elles se contredisent, elles ne sont
plus concordantes et le doute seul peut entrer dans l’esprit du magistrat.

[42]   Les présomptions peuvent
être repoussées par une preuve contraire.

[43] La Cour d’appel dans
Barrette

c.
Union canadienne (L’), compagnie d’assurances
, nous enseigne qu’en
matière de présomption :

[34] L’exercice prévu à l’
article 2849

C.c.Q.
consiste
en deux étapes bien distinctes. La première, établir les faits indiciels. Dans
cette première étape, le juge doit, selon la balance des probabilités, retenir
de la preuve certains faits qu’il estime prouvés. Dans une deuxième étape, il
doit examiner si les faits prouvés et connus l’amènent à conclure, par une
induction puissante, que le fait inconnu est démontré.

[35] Le juge doit se poser trois questions :

1.   Le rapport entre les faits connus et le fait
inconnu permet-il, par induction puissante, de conclure à l’existence de ce
dernier?

2.   Est-il également possible d’en tirer des
conséquences différentes ou même contraires? Si c’est le cas, le fardeau n’est
pas rencontré.

3.   Est-ce que dans leur ensemble, les faits connus
tendent à établir directement et précisément le fait inconnu?

(References omitted)

4.1.2

Application of the principles to the facts of
the case

•

The late Zalac’s condition and his relationship
with the Plaintiff

[
32
]

The late Zalac is described by all the witnesses
as a strong headed, opinionated, and direct person, who spoke his mind loud and
clear about any topic, including day-to-day life, who held nothing back.

[
33
]

The more than thirty-five-year relationship
between him and Ms. Bouchard is described by all witnesses, but Boris
Zalac, his spouse Gilles Bourgeois, and Richard Zalac, as a loving and caring
one with only a few quarrels about little things, except for a period where the
couple’s financial situation was a bit precarious. The late Zalac never kept a
secret from Ms. Bouchard.

[
34
]

It was in the late Zalac’s character to care for
his spouses. For instance, after his divorce, he left the family residence to
his first wife without claiming his share and always paid support. As to the
mother of his third son, he purchased her a house in Poland after the
separation and shipped her furniture.

[
35
]

The relationship took a bad turn around 2019–2020,
with the increasing deterioration of the late Zalac’s health condition. Indeed,
he had lost vision in his right eye following a stroke in 2008, but then
suffered a sudden severe decline in his left eye following cataract surgery in
2019 to the point that he was declared legally blind in 2020 from macular
degeneration
[6]
. Consequently, he experienced difficulties in his life habits, not
being able to cook (one of his favourite activities), to care for his pets, to
do gardening, to read without a magnifying glass, to drive (he used to drive
Ms. Bouchard to work every day), to identify people, and requiring
assistance in his daily life activities. He would sit on a couch near the
window for hours and would wait for Ms. Bouchard to come home after work.
He barely ate.

[
36
]

The late Zalac also suffered from pain in his
hip which limited his mobility and for which he needed surgery, as well as from
hearing impairment.

[
37
]

As a result, as of 2019, the late Zalac would
rarely leave the house, and would become angry, frustrated, and depressed, taking
it out on Ms. Bouchard. He used to be proud and take care of his
appearance, but as of 2020, he neglected his hygiene and did not change his
clothes. He felt worthless and hopeless at what he considered a poor quality of
life.

[
38
]

The 2019–2020 years were difficult, and both Ms. Bouchard
and the late Zalac increased drastically their alcohol drinking, which did not
help their communication. Ms. Bouchard did confide in Boris Zalac of some
marital issues.

[
39
]

The Court grants credibility to the testimonies
of Ms. Bouchard (who candidly admitted to the challenges in her marriage
post 2019, including her drinking), Mr. Michael Meduri (a cousin, neighbour
and friend who spent ample time with the late Zalac), and Ms. Linda
Ritchie (also a cousin and neighbour who used to drive the late Zalac to the
hospital for his appointments since Ms. Bouchard did not drive). Those
last two independent witnesses corroborated for the most part Ms. Bouchard’s
testimony, as to the state of her relationship with the late Zalac.

[
40
]

However, the Court does not believe the
testimony of Boris Zalac who in the total lack of evidence pictured the
relationship between Ms. Bouchard and his father as one that has been “
toxic
” for the most part. The text messages between himself
and Ms. Bouchard that he produced in support of his position (in which she
complains to him of the way the late Zalac is treating her) are all dated post 2019,
which suggests that there was nothing worrying to report before. Moreover, the
preponderant evidence does not support Boris Zalac’s testimony as to the nature
of his relationship with his father, which, for the years before 2020, proved
to be far from the close one that he described. Indeed, in reference to his estranged
sons, the late Zalac would state that he does not have a family. For instance, his
sons barely kept in contact with him, and he did not even invite them to his
wedding with Ms. Bouchard in 2001. Richard Zalac was and is still living
in California; Steve Zalac lived in Belize for many years. However, Boris Zalac
lived in Montreal, but never invited his father or Ms. Bouchard to his
house.

[
41
]

The Court does not believe either Richard Zalac who
went as far as stating that Ms. Bouchard was “
trying to kill
” the
late Zalac.

[
42
]

The preponderant evidence also shows that the
pandemic negatively impacted the late Zalac. He did not understand the gravity
of the pandemic and thought he could still travel to Florida.

•

The circumstances surrounding the 2020 Will

[
43
]

On March 11, 2020, the World Health Organization
declared a COVID-19 pandemic. Following that declaration, governments adopted emergency
measures to protect the population health. The aeronautical industry was hard
hit with a global lockdown. Boris Zalac who worked as a flight attendant at Air
Canada was laid off.

[
44
]

As for Plaintiff, she stopped working in March
due to the lockdown and resumed work in June 2020. During that period,
discussions about modifying the 2015 Wills took place between her and the late
Zalac. Ms. Bouchard who thought that there was only one 2015 will for the
two spouses wanted to remove her niece Tara as a legatee and only keep her
niece Melissa.

[
45
]

Boris Zalac got involved in those discussions
and retained the services of his notary Erika Teesdale who had notarized the
transaction for the acquisition of his condominium a few years before. He
booked an appointment for his father at his notary’s office for April 20, 2020.
However, Ms. Bouchard asked him to cancel it as the late Zalac was not
feeling well. Three other appointments were made (May 14, June 9 and July 7,
2020), all of which were cancelled.

[
46
]

Notary Teesdale testified that she called the
late Zalac on April 29, 2020, to take his instructions for the will and
mandate. Given the late Zalac’s hearing impairment, the Court finds it
difficult to believe, especially since Ms. Bouchard was not back at work
due to COVID-19, and was at home during the day.

[
47
]

On May 13, notary Teesdale emailed the draft
will and draft mandate in case of incapacity to Boris Zalac for review. At that
point, the late Zalac read documents with the help of a flashlight in
combination with corrective glasses, or with a magnifier.

[
48
]

On May 14, notary Teesdale sent her invoice in
the amount of $402.42 to Boris Zalac, who forwarded it for payment to Ms. Bouchard.
The later paid the invoice by cheque thinking her husband was being charged for
the two missed appointments.

[
49
]

On September 24, 2020, Boris Zalac brought his
father to the notary for the signing of the 2020 Will. The meeting took place
in the notary’s office furnished with a long conference table. The late Zalac
sat at one end of the table with Boris Zalac and Mr. Bourgeois, while the
notary sat at the other end. Everyone was wearing a mask due to COVID-19. The
notary gave a copy of the documents to the late Zalac, did not read them, but
gave him the gist. No changes were brought at the meeting, and the late Zalac
signed the 2020 Will as well as the mandate in case of incapacity. Gilles
Bourgeois, Boris Zalac’s spouse, acted as a witness.

[
50
]

Ms. Bouchard who had resumed work in June was
not made aware of the signing of a new will. On February 11, 2021, she suggested
to Boris Zalac to bring her husband to their former notary to alter the 2015
Wills. Her text message remained unanswered.

[
51
]

The Court is very aware that suspicious
behaviour or the active participation of a legatee in the testamentary process
does not make for undue influence. But here, the set of events taken together leads
to the only possible powerful inference, leaving no room for an alternate
conclusion: Boris Zalac took advantage of his father’s vulnerability, weakened medical
condition, isolation, and frustration to make him change his 2015 Will and
leave his entire estate to him.

[
52
]

Several signs of undue influence as enumerated
in the above-mentioned case
M.P.
v.
F.D
are present here: to name
a few, Boris Zalac pressured his father into going to the notary (he would
harass him with phone calls), booked several appointments and following up to make
sure the 2015 Will’s alteration got done, approved the content of the draft of
the new will and mandate in case of incapacity, chose his spouse as the
witness, is the only heir and liquidator, all that with the complacency of the
notary who, incidentally, did not even notice the late Zalac’s hearing and
reading impairments. The late Zalac remained almost mute at the meeting,
keeping his answers to the notary to a short: “
yes
.”

[
53
]

Boris Zalac contends that his father kept his
testamentary intentions confidential to avoid a volatile conflict and tension
at home. This assertion is gratuitous because the evidence does not show that
the late Zalac feared his wife’s reactions. On the contrary, he spoke his mind.

[
54
]

Moreover, Boris Zalac suggests that the fact
that he is the only heir is explained by the fact that his father trusted him
to divide up with his brothers and to take care of Ms. Bouchard.
Considering the testimonies about the late Zalac’s character, it is unlikely that
he would have bequeathed all his property to one son and entrusted him to take care
of his wife and two other sons. At the very least, he would have left
instructions, especially regarding the family residence he co-owned with Ms. Bouchard
and which had always been in her family. Boris Zalac was not homeless; he
already owned a condominium with his common-law spouse. A man like the late
Zalac who had always made decisions for himself would not have relied on his
son to decide on the distribution of his estate. He would have expressed his
last wishes loud and clear, and he did in the 2015 Will. Boris Zalac’s
contention is so far-fetched that it just doesn't hold up.

[
55
]

In the Court’s opinion, Boris Zalac exploited his
father within the meaning of
section 48
of the
Charter of Human Rights and
Freedoms
[7]
:

48.

Every aged person and every handicapped person has a right to protection
against any form of exploitation.

Such a person also has a right to
the protection and security that must be provided to him by his family or the
persons acting in their stead.

[
56
]

The Court will order him to reimburse expenses
he wrongfully paid with the Estate’s patrimony.

4.2

Unworthiness of inheriting

[
57
]

Although the Plaintiff did not address that
issue in her closing arguments, in her Application, she is asking the Court to
declare that Boris Zalac is unworthy of benefiting from his father.
Articles 621

to
623
of the
Civil Code of Quebec
provide:

621.
The following persons may be declared unworthy of inheriting:

(1) a person who has subjected the
deceased to ill-treatment or who has otherwise behaved towards him in a
seriously reprehensible manner;

(2) a person who has concealed,
altered or destroyed in bad faith the will of the deceased;

(3) a person who has hindered the
testator in the drawing up, amendment or revocation of his will.

622.

An heir is not unworthy of inheriting nor subject to being declared so if the
deceased knew the cause of unworthiness and yet conferred a benefit on him or
did not modify the liberality when he could have done so.

623.

Any successor may, within one year after the opening of the succession or
becoming aware of a cause of unworthiness, apply to the court to have an heir
declared unworthy of inheriting if that heir is not unworthy by operation of
law.

[
58
]

Considering its conclusion about the presence of
undue influence, the Court will declare the 2020 Will null and void and order
the devolution of the succession of the late Zalac in virtue of the 2015 Will.
Since that will does not make Boris Zalac a legatee, the conclusion that he be
declared unworthy of inheriting is moot.

[
59
]

Moreover, that conclusion having been added in
the Modified Application dated July 22, 2022, it must fail because the
Plaintiff did not apply within one year after the opening of the succession or
becoming aware of a cause of unworthiness.
